title: 2.3 · Gauge, diameter and area
concept: AWG is a geometric size series. A larger number means a smaller solid conductor. Decreasing by three numbers approximately doubles cross-sectional area. It is not a count of actual manufacturing die passes. Two steps and four steps are different comparisons.

work: A = pi x d² / 4 = pi x 4 / 4.
answer: A is about 3.14 mm²; diameter and area have different units.
question: 10 AWG compared with 14 AWG is how many gauge steps?
options: Four, so area is about 2.53 times as large.
activity: Use disconnected bare solid wire; do not include insulation in conductor diameter.
Measure at three orientations without squeezing. Compare to labelled reference dimensions.
Calculate area from diameter. Compare 14, 12 and 10 AWG reference areas shown.

title: 2.2 · Convert the same slope
concept: A ratio requires matching length units. One quarter inch per foot means 0.25 inch per 12 inches. It is different from 1:12 and from a 4-in-12 roof pitch. Always define whether a written ratio means rise:run.
given: Slope = 1/4 inch per foot.
answer: Equivalent forms: 1/4 in/ft, rise:run 1:48, about 2.083%.
question: Which percent matches 1/4 inch per foot?
activity: Draw triangles for 1/4 in over 12 in, 1 in over 12 in, and 4 in over 12 in.
Convert each into rise:run and percent using matching units.
Exchange tables and reconstruct one original triangle from the labels.
Diagnose a card that labels one triangle both 1/4 in/ft and 8.3%.
exit: Convert 1/8 inch per foot to a rise:run ratio and percent. Explain why 1:12 means a different slope.
exitkey: 1:96 and about 1.0417%. 1:12 is 1 inch per foot, about 8.333%, eight times as steep.
draw: Draw one triangle and annotate three equivalent labels with their units.
materials: Paper, ruler, calculator after setup is shown.
fallback: All quantities are supplied classroom data.

title: 2.3 · Investigate slope and transport
concept: Ask how slope affects transport in this model. Geometry, release conditions, water amount and test material affect results. Do not assume all steeper slopes clog or that an open trough establishes a universal maximum for real drainage.
given: Horizontal model run 24 in = 2 ft; chosen slope 1/4 in/ft.
answer: Measure the setting; do not choose slope by eye.
question: Which test best isolates slope?
options: Change slope, material and water volume together.
Change slope while keeping other planned conditions consistent and repeat trials.
Keep only the result that matches your prediction.
activity: If water is permitted, use a contained tray and identical releases; otherwise use a dry bead/ramp model and label the changed model.
Set at least three slopes by measured rise and run. Record transport distance or stopping position.
Repeat each setting three times; keep release, material, volume if used, and observation time consistent.
Compare the observations and name limits before applying them to another system.
exit: A class reports no decline in transport at its steepest tested setting. What can they conclude, and what can they not conclude? Propose a useful next test.
exitkey: Report no decline over these tested conditions; do not invent a maximum or conclude no maximum exists in all systems. Repeat trials or extend one controlled variable and predict measurable outcomes.
draw: Draw the apparatus with measured run, rise, release point and measurement endpoint.
materials: Dry ramp, bead, tray and ruler; optional teacher-approved contained water trough.
fallback: Analyze supplied trial data: at slopes 1/8, 1/4, 1/2 in/ft, distances 12/13/11, 18/19/18, 22/24/23 in. These are simulated examples.

title: 2.4 · Budget the depth
concept: A drain route consumes vertical depth through fall and its complete outside envelope. Include stated clearances. Geometric feasibility is separate from permission to drill, notch or change structure.
given: Dry bay: run 16 ft; slope 1/4 in/ft; OD 2 3/8 in; top and bottom clearances 1 in each.
answer: A 7 1/2-inch available depth is short by 7/8 inch.
question: Which calculation includes the whole depth demand?
options: Pipe OD plus fall plus both specified clearances.
activity: List run, slope requirement, OD, clearances and available depth before calculating.
Build a paper envelope model; keep all elevations on one datum.
Test one route change at a time and recalculate.
State which change requires coordination with another trade or approval.
exit: Keep the example OD and clearances. With 7 1/2 inches of depth and 1/4 in/ft slope, what is the maximum horizontal run in this geometric model?
exitkey: Available fall = 7.5 - 2.375 - 2 = 3.125 in. Maximum run = 3.125/0.25 = 12.5 ft. This is not authorization to alter framing.
draw: Draw the outside envelope through the bay and label the four depth components.
materials: Paper bay strip, ruler, calculator.
fallback: Use the exact supplied dimensions; no real pipe or framing modification.

title: 2.5 · Draw the fall
concept: A plan locates the route horizontally; a longitudinal section communicates elevations and fall. Link the views with the same labels and datum. Write a slope note and flow direction so a reader does not have to infer them from the sketch angle.
given: Route A to B is 12 ft horizontally. A elevation 30 in; required slope 1/4 in/ft.
answer: B elevation is 27 in on the same datum.
question: Which pair of views communicates this route best?
options: Plan alone with a diagonal-looking line.
Linked plan and longitudinal section with dimensions and common datum.
activity: Draw a plan locating A and B and label the horizontal run.
Draw the corresponding section with both endpoint elevations and outside pipe envelope.
Add flow arrow, slope note, datum and scale or NTS.
Give it to a partner who computes fall independently; revise ambiguous information.
exit: A plan calls for 12 ft at 1/4 in/ft, but its section labels A 30 in and B 28 in. Identify the conflict and two ways to make the documentation internally consistent without reducing the required slope.
exitkey: Required fall 3 in, drawn fall 2. If A fixed, B must be 27; if B fixed, A must be 31. Check which endpoints can actually move; do not claim either is approved.
draw: Submit matching plan and section with A/B labels, common datum, elevations, flow and required slope.
materials: Graph paper, ruler; Drawing Book plan/section reference.
fallback: Use the supplied route; state that feasibility at a real bay is unverified.

title: 3.1 · When the floor finish changes
concept: First and last risers meet floor finishes that may change after stair layout. This is one possible cause of unequal rises, not an automatic diagnosis. Separate the original surfaces, added finish thickness and finished walking surfaces.
given: Original end rises both 7 1/2 in. Add 3/4 in finish at bottom floor only.
answer: Raising the bottom walking surface reduces the first rise.
question: Add 3/4 inch at the upper landing only. What happens to the last rise?
activity: Model the stair with paper strips and marked original walking surfaces.
Add a measured finish strip at the bottom, then separately at the upper landing.
Predict before measuring each new rise. Keep other surfaces unchanged.
Draw before/after sections and identify information needed to investigate an actual stair.
exit: Both ends originally have 7 1/2-inch rises. Add 1/2 inch at the bottom floor and 3/4 inch at the upper landing. Predict the new end rises and a check.
exitkey: First 7 in; last 8 1/4 in, assuming tread surfaces unchanged. Verify finish thickness, endpoints and actual elevations before attributing a real variation.
draw: Show original and finished floor lines, added thickness and new end rises.
materials: Cardboard steps or paper section, measured strips, rule.
fallback: Use labelled before/after diagrams and supplied thicknesses.

title: 3.2 · Rack the frame
concept: A hinged four-sided frame can change angles while keeping side lengths. A diagonal constrains that motion through a triangular geometry. Real performance also depends on connections, member behavior and anchorage; a classroom brace is not a structural design.
given: Rectangle model 3 units by 4 units.
work: Its square diagonal is 5 units. A fixed 5-unit diagonal ties those three lengths together.
answer: The triangle constrains shape when its members and connections hold their lengths.
question: Why does a diagonal help a hinged rectangular model?
options: It creates a triangle with constrained side lengths.
It makes all connections infinitely strong.
activity: Make a small card-strip frame with freely moving joints. Apply a gentle sideways push.
Measure both diagonals before and after; keep side lengths unchanged.
Add a diagonal strip and repeat the same gentle comparison.
Observe the joints; explain how looseness changes the result.
exit: A braced model still shifts. Give two plausible causes and tests that distinguish them before adding another brace.
exitkey: Connection slip versus brace stretch/buckling or unanchored base. Mark joints, compare diagonal length and track base motion; predict which measurement changes for each cause.
draw: Draw the displaced and braced frames. Mark the diagonal and the joints you inspected.
materials: Card strips, paper fasteners/tape hinges, ruler.
fallback: Use supplied before/after diagonal readings and clearly mark model-only evidence.

title: 3.3 · The bay is already full
concept: A coordinated route must satisfy all stated constraints at once. Preserve the required slope and fixed interfaces while examining changes to route length, elevation or available envelope. A supported infeasibility finding is a valid result.
given: Practice bay: 7.5 in deep; 16 ft route; 0.25 in/ft slope; OD 2.375 in; clearances 1 in top and bottom.
work: Required depth 8.375 in; available 7.5. Shortfall = 0.875 in.
answer: The route does not fit this supplied envelope as drawn.
question: Which response resolves the calculation honestly?
options: Report the shortfall and calculate a permitted alternative for review.
Ignore pipe OD because it is small.
activity: Read every constraint aloud and label which interfaces are fixed.
Draw the longitudinal outside envelope and prove the conflict numerically.
Compare shorter run, deeper service zone and changed endpoint options.
Assign trade roles for discussion; each student writes an individual recommendation and its consequence.
exit: The case allows either a 12-foot run or a deeper service zone. Calculate the depth needed for the 12-foot option and explain what else must be checked before choosing it.
exitkey: Fall 3 in; total depth 7.375 in, fitting 7.5 with 0.125 in remaining. Need routing/access, fittings and connection feasibility; the remaining margin may be insufficient once those are specified.
draw: Draw existing and proposed routes with labelled changed constraints and an RFI note.
materials: Practice bay case, paper, ruler; Drawing Set S-102/P-201 for optional comparison.
fallback: Complete the paper coordination case; do not infer field dimensions.

title: 3.4 · Call it, then check it
concept: An estimate is useful when followed by a measurement. Keep prediction, measured result and revised explanation as separate records. A slope that looks nearly level can still have a meaningful fall over a long run.
given: Three model runs are 4 ft. Supplied falls are 1/2, 1 and 2 in.
answer: Slopes are 1/8, 1/4 and 1/2 in/ft.
question: A 4-foot model needs 1/4 in/ft slope. What fall should you set?
activity: Prepare three dry strips with different slopes. Hide the measured fall values initially.
Predict which matches a stated requirement, then measure horizontal run and fall.
Calculate each slope; keep the original prediction visible.
Explain one mismatch and adjust one strip to the required slope.
exit: A 6-foot model falls 1 1/8 inches. Calculate slope and the change in fall needed to reach 1/4 in/ft.
exitkey: Slope 3/16 in/ft. Required fall 1.5 in; increase fall by 3/8 in. State which endpoint moves and the datum.
draw: Draw your adjusted model with measured horizontal run and before/after elevations.
materials: Three dry strips, blocks, ruler, checked level reference.
fallback: Use the supplied falls with predictions recorded before calculation.

title: 3.5 · Mastery: route it and prove it
concept: Your report must show either a feasible route under every supplied condition or a quantified conflict and a revision for review. A changed drawing must still communicate the required slope, outside envelope and fixed interfaces.
given: Practice calculation: run 10 ft, slope 1/4 in/ft, OD 2 3/8 in, top and bottom clearances 3/4 in.
answer: Required depth 6 5/8 in. Use the different values on Case B for the assessed task.
question: What makes “it cannot fit as drawn” a valid conclusion?
options: A calculation showing the violated constraint and the amount.
activity: Read Classroom Case B and write the fixed and changeable conditions.
Calculate fall and full depth demand; draw matching plan and section.
Evaluate both offered revisions, then recommend one with an explicit remaining check.
Submit an individual report and drawing. After feedback, revise only with identified new or corrected evidence.
exit: Summarize your Case B decision: quantified conflict, recommended revision, consequence for another trade, and the measurement or approval still required.
exitkey: Use Case B key: 18-foot original needs 8 3/8 inches and exceeds 8 by 3/8. Shorter 16-foot route needs 7 7/8; deeper 8 1/2-inch zone fits original with 1/8 margin. Neither margin includes unspecified fittings.
draw: Submit your linked plan and longitudinal section, with common datum, slope, flow direction and full envelope.
materials: Case B pages, paper, ruler, calculator; optional dry classroom bay mockup.
fallback: Use the supplied case and keep instrument performance not observed.
